newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania rebels gain ground, but Italy brokers truce.
newsitem.headline: Albania rebels gain ground, but Italy brokers truce.

text.p: Rebels dismissing President Berisha's political deal to end Albania's conflict have made big gains in southern regions, but Italy brokered a deal to end confrontation in the port serving as the revolt's focal point.
Insurgents insisting they would down no arms until Berisha resigned took over a string of towns in the volatile south, frequently encountering no resistance from army troops.
The latest areas to fall into their hands included the ancient town of Berat, nearby Kucove, site of one of two big Albanian air force bases, and Permet, a remote mountain town.

But representatives of rebels controlling the port of Vlore, site of some of Albania's fiercest rioting, signed a declaration seeking quick implementation of the weekend accord signed by Berisha and opposition parties.
The deal calls for an all-party government, elections by June and an amnesty for anyone handing in arms within a week.

"The committee...undertook to favour the immediate handing back of weapons in the hands of the citizens of Vlore and to ensure public order and progessively restore normal administration to the town," the declaration said.
The statement, issued by the Italian Foreign Ministry and read on Albanian television, was signed on an Italian warship in the Adriatic after talks with Italy's ambassador to Tirana.
In Washington, the U.S. State Department welcomed the peace efforts and called on the rebels in the south to lay down their arms.
At least 40 people have died in the latest wave of disturbances over the past 10 days.

Parliament initially proclaimed a state of emergency and then re-elected Berisha to a second five-year term before talks on a political deal were launched at the urging of two top-level European mediation teams.
Italy clearly views disarming the rebels as a key element in ensuring stability and preventing a repeat of mass departures of refugees across the sea in the early 1990s.

It was not clear how the undertaking would be carried out in Vlore -- where the latest wave of violence erupted more than a week ago. Nor was it certain to have any effect on any other areas in the volatile south.
In Tirana, fresh talks produced an agreement to share ministerial posts equally between government and opposition parties in an interim government responsible for overseeing elections by June.
The prime minister was to be chosen by Berisha and his deputy by the opposition, led by the former Socialists, heirs to the Communists who ran eastern Europe's harshest post-war regime for 45 years.
Rebels in most of the southern areas now under the control of anti-government groups were having none of it.
"Down with Berisha, down with the murderer!" chanted a crowd of 3,000 at the funerals of some of the five people who died in clashes preceding the rebel capture of Permet.

Reactions were similar in Berat, though the town was taken without a fight after soldiers fled. "We don't trust him any more," said Sokol, one of the rebels trying to maintain order in the town. "He deserves to be hanged by the tongue."
Many rebels accuse Berisha of doing nothing to warn unwary investors of the pitfalls of pyramid investment schemes. Five have collapsed with the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people.

Reports reaching Tirana said at least two more southern towns, Polican and Corovode, had fallen into rebel hands. Army and police roadblocks were removed on the main highway south of the Shkumbini River bisecting Albania.
